pron:er.tx: From Middle High German ër, from Old High German ër, from Proto-West Germanic *iʀ, from Proto-Germanic *iz. In northern Middle High German and Old High German there also existed forms with initial h-, namely Middle High German hër, Old High German hër, from Proto-Germanic *hiz, whence Central Franconian hä and (from the accusative) Luxembourgish hien. Compare English he. The unusual spelling ih- …

adj:eng.tx: From Middle High German enge, from Old High German engi, from Proto-West Germanic *angī.

num:elf.tx: From Middle High German eilf, eilef, einlif, from Old High German einlif, from Proto-Germanic *ainalif, a compound of *ainaz and *-lif. Until the 19th century usually written eilf; the monophthongal form is of Central and Low German origin (Middle Low German elf). Compare Dutch elf, West Frisian alve, English eleven, Danish elleve.

pron:es.tx: From Middle High German ëȥ, from Old High German iȥ, from Proto-Germanic *it (“it”). Compare English it, which instead descends from Proto-Germanic *hit (“it”). Cognate with Yiddish עס (es).

adj:echt.tx: From Middle High German echt, borrowed from Middle Low German echt (“lawful, genuine”). The original form is Middle Low German ēhaft (“lawful”), from ē (“law”) (related to modern Ehe); then ēhacht by the Low German development -ft- → -cht- (compare Nichte); and eventually contracted into echt. Cognate to Old High German ēhaft (“honourable”), Alemannic German ächt and Dutch echt.

adv:echt.tx: From Middle High German echt, borrowed from Middle Low German echt (“lawful, genuine”). The original form is Middle Low German ēhaft (“lawful”), from ē (“law”) (related to modern Ehe); then ēhacht by the Low German development -ft- → -cht- (compare Nichte); and eventually contracted into echt. Cognate to Old High German ēhaft (“honourable”), Alemannic German ächt and Dutch echt.

intj:echt.tx: From Middle High German echt, borrowed from Middle Low German echt (“lawful, genuine”). The original form is Middle Low German ēhaft (“lawful”), from ē (“law”) (related to modern Ehe); then ēhacht by the Low German development -ft- → -cht- (compare Nichte); and eventually contracted into echt. Cognate to Old High German ēhaft (“honourable”), Alemannic German ächt and Dutch echt.

intj:ei.tx: For the “caressing” sense compare Dutch aaien.

adj:englisch.tx: From Engl(and) (“England”) + -isch, or Middle High German englisch, or borrowed directly from English English.

pron:etwas.tx: From Middle High German etewaʒ, from Old High German eddeshwaz, from edde- + hwaz. The first element is of obscure origin, but possibly related to Proto-Germanic *ehþau (“otherwise, or, but if”), source of modern oder (“or”). Compare Icelandic eitthvað, Dutch ietwat.

adv:etwas.tx: From Middle High German etewaʒ, from Old High German eddeshwaz, from edde- + hwaz. The first element is of obscure origin, but possibly related to Proto-Germanic *ehþau (“otherwise, or, but if”), source of modern oder (“or”). Compare Icelandic eitthvað, Dutch ietwat.

det:etwas.tx: From Middle High German etewaʒ, from Old High German eddeshwaz, from edde- + hwaz. The first element is of obscure origin, but possibly related to Proto-Germanic *ehþau (“otherwise, or, but if”), source of modern oder (“or”). Compare Icelandic eitthvað, Dutch ietwat.

noun:Ehebruch.tx: From late Middle High German ēbruch. Analysable as Ehe (“marriage”) + Bruch (“breach, breaking”).

adj:eigen.tx: From Middle High German eigen, from Old High German eigan, from Proto-West Germanic *aigan, from Proto-Germanic *aiganaz, the past participle of Proto-Germanic *aiganą. Cognate with Dutch eigen, English own.

noun:Eisen.tx: From Middle High German īsen, īsern, from Old High German īsarn, from Proto-West Germanic *īsarn, from Proto-Germanic *īsarną, from Proto-Celtic *īsarnom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”). Cognate with Dutch ijzer, Alemannic German Ise, English iron, Danish jern.

verb:eggen.tx: From Middle High German egen, *ecken, from Old High German eggen, ekken, ultimately from the root of Ecke (“corner, edge”). The modern consonantism -gg- instead of expected -ck- is most readily explained as Low German as some sources do, but this seems not generally accepted (compare Middle Low German eggen).

pron:einander.tx: From Middle High German einander, from Old High German compound of ein (“one”) + andar (“other”, modern German ander). Semantically limited by the ein (“one”) to singular contexts, similar to one another or each other. The combined form einander does not inflect in modern German, and may be used unchanged in dative and accusative grammatical cases. Older forms could show inflection on the second …

num:ein.tx: From Middle High German ein, from Old High German ein. Compare Low German en, een, ein, Dutch een, English one, Danish en, Norwegian Nynorsk ein.

det:ein.tx: From Middle High German ein, from Old High German ein. Compare Low German en, een, ein, Dutch een, English one, Danish en, Norwegian Nynorsk ein.

adv:ein.tx: Related to in, from Old High German in, from Proto-Germanic *in, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én. Compare ein- and English in-.

adj:ein.tx: Related to in, from Old High German in, from Proto-Germanic *in, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én. Compare ein- and English in-.

noun:Eis.tx: From Middle High German īs, from Old High German īs, from Proto-West Germanic *īs, from Proto-Germanic *īsą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyH-. Etymology 1, noun sense 2 is a semantic loan from French glace.

adj:eminent.tx: Borrowed from French éminent, from Latin eminens.

adj:extra.tx: Borrowed from Latin extrā, see also the similarly borrowed prefix extra-. Pfeifer speculates that the standalone usage with the sense of "separate" arises out of phrases like extrā ōrdinem (“out of the ordinary”) which occurs in 16th century German chancellary texts.

adv:extra.tx: Borrowed from Latin extrā, see also the similarly borrowed prefix extra-. Pfeifer speculates that the standalone usage with the sense of "separate" arises out of phrases like extrā ōrdinem (“out of the ordinary”) which occurs in 16th century German chancellary texts.

conj:eh.tx: From Middle High German ē (“earlier, ere”), originally ēr. Modern Standard German uses the lengthened form ehe (only as a conjunction).

adv:eh.tx: From Middle High German ē (“earlier, ere”), originally ēr. Modern Standard German uses the lengthened form ehe (only as a conjunction).

noun:Eber.tx: From Middle High German ëber, from Old High German ëbur, from Proto-West Germanic *ebur, from Proto-Germanic *eburaz, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-r-. Cognate with Dutch ever, Latin aper, Serbo-Croatian vepar. Despite the similarity in form and meaning, not related to obsolete dialectal Bär (“boar”) or to Bär (“bear”).

noun:Exodus.tx: From Middle High German Exodus, from Latin Exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos).

noun:Eid.tx: From Middle High German eit, from Old High German eid, from Proto-West Germanic *aiþ, from Proto-Germanic *aiþaz. Compare Dutch eed, English oath, Danish ed.

verb:erwachsen.tx: From Middle High German erwachsen, from Old High German irwahsan, urwahsan. Equivalent to er- + wachsen.

adj:erwachsen.tx: From Middle High German erwachsen, from Old High German irwahsan, urwahsan. Equivalent to er- + wachsen.

verb:erheben.tx: From Middle High German erheben, from Old High German irheffen, irheven, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀhabbjan, from Proto-Germanic *uzhabjaną. Equivalent to er- + heben. Cognate with Middle Dutch erheffen (whence Dutch verheffen), Old Saxon āhebbian, Old English āhebban, Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌷𐌰𐍆𐌾𐌰𐌽 (ushafjan).

noun:Einstein.tx: The surname is habitational, from any of various places named with a Middle High German derivative of einsteinen ("to enclose or surround with stone"), cp. ein-, Stein and -en, or from ein + Stein. The "an extremely intelligent person" sense is an eponym of Albert Einstein.

verb:essen.tx: From Middle High German ëȥȥen, from Old High German ëȥȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *etan, from Proto-Germanic *etaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-. Cognate with Low German eten, Alemannic German ässe, Dutch eten, English eat, Danish æde, Norwegian ete, Swedish äta, Yiddish עסן (esn) and Gothic 𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (itan). Non-Germanic cognates include Latin edō, Russian есть (jestʹ), Scottish Gaelic ith.

num:eins.tx: Contraction of eines (nominative/accusative neuter of ein), from Middle High German einez, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ainatō, form of *ainaz (“one”).

adv:eins.tx: Contraction of eines (genitive neuter of ein), from Middle High German eines, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ainas, form of *ainaz (“one”). Doublet of einst (“once”). That this use is an original genitive results from the Middle High German spelling as well as from the fact that those dialects with an unshifted final -t in etymology 1 (Central Franconian, Low Franconian, Low German) invariably …

noun:Elysium.tx: From Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἠλῠ́σῐον (Πεδῐ́ον) (Ēlŭ́sĭon (Pedĭ́on)).

noun:Elch.tx: From Middle High German elch, elhe, from Old High German elaho, elho, elcho (hapax elach), from Proto-West Germanic *elh(ō), from Proto-Germanic *elhaz. In Early Modern German, the word had been entirely replaced with Elen (see there). In the late 18th century, the form Elk was borrowed from English elk, principally for the North American moose (then still thus called). This subsequently …

verb:entdecken.tx: From Middle High German endecken, from Old High German intthecken, inthecken. Equivalent to ent- + decken.

noun:Echo.tx: From Latin ēchō, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ).

noun:Ecstasy.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English ecstasy. Doublet of Ekstase.

noun:Ei.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ei and Old High German ei, from Proto-West Germanic *aij, from Proto-Germanic *ajją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm. Cognate with Yiddish איי (ey), Dutch ei, West Frisian aai, English ey and egg, Danish æg.

noun:Eider.tx: 18th century, from Icelandic æður, from Old Norse æðr, probably reaching German via Swedish eider (now ejder), from a North Germanic root.

noun:Elefant.tx: From Middle High German elefant, elfant, relatinisation of helfant, from Old High German helfant, from Proto-West Germanic *elpand (“elephant, ivory”).

noun:Element.tx: From Middle High German element, from Latin elementum (see further etymology there).

noun:Elle.tx: From Middle High German elle, from Old High German elina, from Proto-West Germanic *alinu. The form elle is most readily explained as an assimilation of syncopated elne (like müller from earlier mülnære). Alternatively it can also be a backformation from apocopated eln, elen. Cognate with English ell, which compare.

noun:Embryo.tx: 15th century, from Latin embryo, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon).

noun:Emu.tx: Probably from Portuguese ema (“ostrich”), of unknown origin.

noun:Engel.tx: From Middle High German engel, from Old High German engil from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos). Cognate with English angel.

noun:Enkel.tx: From Middle High German enkel, from Old High German enkil, enchil, Proto-West Germanic *ankil, *ankul, from Proto-Germanic *ankulaz (“ankle”). Cognate with Dutch enkel, English ankle.

noun:Ente.tx: From Middle High German ente, confluence of (1.) the plural and oblique singular of ant and (2.) the Old High German variant enita, both from older anut, from Proto-West Germanic *anad. Cognate with Dutch eend. The sense “canard” (mid-19th c.) is a calque of French canard, but also ties in with the expression blaue Enten (“lies, humbug”, literally “blue ducks”, since 15th c.). The sense “Citroën …

noun:Episode.tx: Borrowed from French épisode, from Ancient Greek ἐπεισόδιον (epeisódion).

noun:Ersatz.tx: Back-formation from ersetzen (“to replace, to substitute”).

noun:Esprit.tx: Borrowed from French esprit. Doublet of Spirit and Sprit.

noun:Esse.tx: From Middle High German esse, from Old High German essa (“furnace”), from Proto-Germanic *asjǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs- (“to dry, burn, glow; hearth, ashes”). Related to Asche, English ash.

noun:Essen.tx: From Middle High German ëȥȥen, from Old High German ëȥȥan, akin to Old Saxon etan, compare Dutch eten.

noun:Ester.tx: Probably a blend of Essig (“vinegar, acetic acid”) + Äther (“ether”), though this is speculative.

noun:Etymologie.tx: Borrowed from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología).

noun:Eunuch.tx: In Germanised form since ca. 1600, from Late Middle High German eunuchus, from Latin eunūchus, from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos).

noun:Evangelist.tx: From Latin evangelista, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistḗs).

noun:Erbse.tx: From Middle High German erbīz, erwīz, arwīz, ar(e)weiz, from Old High German arawīz, araweiz, from Proto-West Germanic *arwīt, *arwait. Cognate with Dutch erwt, Swedish ärta.

verb:entfliehen.tx: From Middle High German entvliehen. Equivalent to ent- (“parting something”) + fliehen (“to flee”).

noun:Ecke.tx: From Middle High German ecke, from Old High German egga, from Proto-West Germanic *aggju, from Proto-Germanic *agjō. Compare English edge.

noun:Eisenbahn.tx: From Eisen (“iron”) + Bahn (“transport, lane”), originally for the iron rails of trains used in mining.

noun:Erde.tx: From Middle High German ërde, from Old High German ërda, from Proto-West Germanic *erþu, from Proto-Germanic *erþō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁érteh₂ (“earth”). Compare Bavarian Erdn, Alemannic German Erde, Dutch aarde, West Frisian ierde, Low German Eerde, English earth, Danish jord, Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌸𐌰 (airþa).

noun:Erdbirne.tx: From Erde (“earth”) + Birne (“pear”). Perhaps an alteration of Erdapfel (literally “earth-apple”), as Erdbirne originally referred specifically to potatoes with an oblong shape, closer to that of a pear than an apple.

noun:Elen.tx: From Middle High German eln, elent (mid-13th c.), of uncertain origin. Often derived from Old Lithuanian elenis (“deer”, modern élnias), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁el-. This derivation is supported by the fact that the el(e)n form appears during a time when the elk was gradually dying out in the German-speaking lands. However, it must be noted that the Lithuanian word does not refer to the elk …

verb:einlassen.tx: From Middle High German īnlāȥen, from Old High German inlāȥan. Equivalent to ein- (“in”) + lassen (“to let”).

verb:entführen.tx: From Middle High German entvüeren (also enphüeren), from Old High German intfuoren. By surface analysis, ent- + führen, literally “to lead off, to take away”. Formed similarly to Latin abducere, but the Old High German translates other Latin verbs, so a calque must remain speculative. Compare Dutch ontvoeren.

verb:erzählen.tx: From Middle High German erzellen, from Old High German irzellen. Equivalent to er- + zählen.

noun:Eule.tx: From Middle High German iule, iuwel, from Old High German ūwila, from Proto-West Germanic *uwwulā (“owl”).

intj:ey.tx: Derived from Middle High German ei, a common interjection. In contemporary German possibly reinforced by Turkish ey (“vocative particle”), English hey.

verb:entsagen.tx: From ent- + sagen, cognate with Dutch ontzeggen.

verb:entbehren.tx: From Middle High German enbërn, from Old High German inbëran. Equivalent to the prefix ent- + *behren, an obsolete verb ultimately from the root of gebären (“to give birth”). Cognate with Luxembourgish entbieren, Dutch ontberen.

noun:Eifersucht.tx: From Eifer (“eagerness, zeal, alacrity”) + Sucht (“anxiety; sickness; addiction”).

noun:Eifer.tx: From Middle High German *īver (“jealousy”). The simplex is first attested in 1494 as yfer, but in 1349 the derivative eifrær (in a southern text that already reflects diphthongisation, thus equivalent to a classical *īverære). An Upper German dialect word, which was chosen by Luther to express the idea of Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos). From the German then Dutch ijver, Middle Low German īver, and …

noun:Essig.tx: Originally a mistaken spelling of German Essich, from Middle High German eȥȥich, from Old High German eȥȥih, from Proto-West Germanic *atek, metathesized variant of *aket (“vinegar”). Cognate with Luxembourgish Esseg and Vilamovian essig.

noun:Erdbeere.tx: By surface analysis, Erde (“earth”) + Beere (“berry”); from Middle High German ërtbere, from Old High German ërdberi, from Proto-Germanic *erþōbazją. Akin to Dutch aardbei, Danish jordbær. Compare Polish poziomka, Russian земляни́ка (zemljaníka) (related to земля́ (zemljá)).

noun:Elster.tx: From Middle High German elster, alster, agelster, from Old High German agalstra, from Proto-West Germanic *agastrijā (“magpie”).

noun:Eichhörnchen.tx: From Eichhorn (“squirrel”) + -chen (“diminutive suffix”), folk etymology based on Eiche and Horn, but actually from Middle High German eichurne, from Old High German eihhorno, from Proto-West Germanic *aikwernō. Cognate with Dutch eekhoorn, eekhoorntje, West Frisian iikhoarntsje, Middle English aquerne, Danish egern, Norwegian Bokmål ekorn, Swedish ekorre, Icelandic íkorni. Possibly related to …

noun:Eichhorn.tx: Inherited from Middle High German eichurne, eichorn. See Eichhörnchen for more.

noun:Eiche.tx: From Middle High German eich, from Old High German eih. Cognates Compare Low German Eek, Dutch eik, West Frisian iik, English oak, Danish eg, Swedish ek, and more distantly Latin aesculus (“Durmast oak”), Latvian ozols, Lithuanian ąžuolas, and Albanian enjë (“juniper, yew”).

noun:Erzbischof.tx: From Middle High German erzebischof, from Old High German erzibiscof. erz- + Bischof

verb:erwürgen.tx: From Middle High German erwürgen, from Old High German irwurgen. Equivalent to er- + würgen (“to choke”). The main sense has always been “strangle”. In Early Modern German it was generalised to “kill, murder”, but this use was shortlived.

noun:Erdmännchen.tx: From Erde (“earth, ground”) + Männchen (“little man”). The original sense is that of a gnome, though the word was also used metaphorically or jocularly for animals in some dialects, e.g. for the mole. The use for “meerkat” has only become established in scientific use since the 1960s, but is older in Namibian German, where it also referred to the similar-looking Cape ground squirrel (Xerus …

adv:einmal.tx: From Middle High German einmāle, equivalent to ein + -mal. Compare Middle Low German ênmâl.

adv:entgegen.tx: From Middle High German engegen, from Old High German ingegin, ingagan, from Proto-West Germanic *andagagin. Compare Old English onġean (English again), Middle Dutch entegen (Dutch entegen), Old Saxon angegin, Yiddish אַנטקעגן (antkegn).

prep:entgegen.tx: From Middle High German engegen, from Old High German ingegin, ingagan, from Proto-West Germanic *andagagin. Compare Old English onġean (English again), Middle Dutch entegen (Dutch entegen), Old Saxon angegin, Yiddish אַנטקעגן (antkegn).

noun:Eingang.tx: From earlier Ingang, from Middle High German ingang, from Old High German ingang (“entrance”), from Proto-Germanic *inngangaz. Cognate with Dutch ingang (“entrance”), English ingang (“entrance”). More at ingang.

noun:Elfenbein.tx: From Middle High German elfenbein, from Old High German elfantbein, from Proto-West Germanic *elpandabain. Equivalent to Elefant + Bein. The loss of initial h- in early modern German was due to the influence of Latin elephās. Since the 19th century the word has been remotivated, somewhat meaningfully (with regard to the pure white colour of ivory), as Elfe (“elf”) + Bein (“bone”).

noun:Eltern.tx: From Middle High German eltern, from Old High German eltirōn, from Proto-Germanic *alþizô. Compare Dutch ouders, English elders. The form is equivalent to a nominalised comparative of alt (“old”). The according spelling Ältern was common in Early Modern German, but later went out of fashion. Several sources claim that this was due to incomprehension of the etymology, but that seems implausible …

noun:Egel.tx: From Middle High German egel(e), from Old High German egala (8th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *egulā, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *egulaz. Cognate to Dutch echel. Further related with Ancient Greek ἔχις (ékhis), Armenian իժ (iž).

adj:ewig.tx: From Middle High German ēwic, Old High German ēwig, from Old High German ewa (from Proto-Germanic *aiwaz, equivalent to German Ehe) + -ig. Compare Dutch eeuwig.

adv:ewig.tx: From Middle High German ēwic, Old High German ēwig, from Old High German ewa (from Proto-Germanic *aiwaz, equivalent to German Ehe) + -ig. Compare Dutch eeuwig.

adj:ernst.tx: From Middle High German ërnst, from Old High German ërnust, from Proto-West Germanic *ernust, from Proto-Germanic *ernustuz, whence also English earnest.

adj:ehrlich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ērlich, from Old High German ērlīh, from Proto-West Germanic *aiʀulīk. Equivalent to Ehre (“honour”) + -lich (“-ly”).

verb:ebben.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German ebben; see Ebbe.

noun:Erle.tx: From Middle High German erle, from Old High German erila, from Proto-West Germanic *aliʀu, from Proto-Germanic *alizō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élis-. Compare Dutch els, English alder, Danish el, Norwegian older, Icelandic elri.

noun:Erz.tx: From Middle High German arze, erze, from Old High German aruzzi, aruz, from Proto-West Germanic *arut.

verb:errichten.tx: From Middle High German errihten, from Old High German irrihten, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀrihtijan. Equivalent to er- + richten.

verb:erweisen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German erwîsen, equivalent to er- + weisen.

verb:erklären.tx: From Middle High German erklæren. By surface analysis, er- + klären.

noun:Euter.tx: From Middle High German iuter, ūter m or n, from Old High German ūtar, ūtir, ūtiro m, from Proto-Germanic *ūdarą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ówHdʰr̥.

noun:Eiter.tx: From Middle High German eiter, from Old High German eitar, from Proto-West Germanic *aitr.

adv:entlang.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German entlanc, cognate with German in lang (with a gliding sound -t-).

prep:entlang.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German entlanc, cognate with German in lang (with a gliding sound -t-).

noun:Eichel.tx: From Middle High German eichel, from Old High German eihhila, from Proto-West Germanic *aikilā. Equivalent to Eiche (“oak”) + -el, alternative to Proto-West Germanic *-ilā (“fruit of the tree”). The sense “glans penis” is a semantic loan from Latin glāns.

noun:Ende.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ende, from Old High German enti, from Proto-West Germanic *andī, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos.

noun:Egge.tx: Derived in early modern German from the verb eggen, possibly under influence of ecke, also egge (“corner; sharp edge; blade”), whence contemporary Ecke (“corner”). The older Middle High German egede from Old High German egida is only continued dialectally (early modern German eide). The same development in Dutch eg. Cognate to Latin occa, Latin occō (whence Portuguese oco, Spanish hueco).

noun:Efeu.tx: From Middle High German ephöu, from Old High German ebhouwi, derived through popular association with houwi (“hay”) from older ebah. Possibly from Proto-Germanic *ibahs, from Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)ebʰ-. The spelling and pronunciation in modern German used to be Epheu [ˈeːpˌhɔʏ̯]. The contemporary -f- is a spelling pronunciation that emanated from the North, reinforced by forms in Central and …

noun:Erbe.tx: From Middle High German erbe, from Old High German erbi, from Proto-West Germanic *arbī, from Proto-Germanic *arbiją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ- (“to change ownership”). Cognate with Dutch erf (“yard”), obsolete English erf. Related to German Arbeit (“work”).

noun:Ebbe.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German ebbe, from Old Saxon *ebbia, from Proto-West Germanic *abbjā, from Proto-Germanic *abjǭ. Cognate to Dutch eb, English ebb.

noun:Ehe.tx: From Middle High German ē, ēwe, from Old High German ēwa, from Proto-West Germanic *aiw, from Proto-Germanic *aiwǭ, *aiwaz (“law, custom”).

noun:Ehre.tx: From Middle High German ēre, from Old High German ēra (“honour, fame, sense of honour”), from Proto-West Germanic *aiʀu, from Proto-Germanic *aizō. Cognate with Old Norse eir (“pardon, gentleness”), Old Saxon ēra (“honour, protection, pardon, gift”), Old English ār (“honour, help, pardon”), and Latin aes-tumare (“to acknowledge, value”).

noun:Eidechse.tx: From Middle High German eidehse, egdehse, egedehse, from Old High German egidehsa (“lizard”).

noun:Eile.tx: From Middle High German īlaé, from Old High German īla, from Proto-West Germanic *īlu, from Proto-Germanic *īlō (“rush, haste”).

noun:Eimer.tx: From Middle High German eim(b)er, einber, Old High German einber, from Proto-West Germanic *ambrī. Cognate with Luxembourgish Eemer.

noun:Ekel.tx: From Middle Low German ēkel, probably from the verb in German ekeln, which see.

noun:Ellbogen.tx: From Middle High German elenboge, from Old High German elinbogo, from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô; by surface analysis, Elle + Bogen.

noun:Erker.tx: From Middle High German ärkēr (in rhyme with mēr), ärker or ærker (in rhyme with der), ultimately from Latin arcus.

noun:Ernte.tx: From Middle High German erne f (alongside arn m), from Old High German arn f, from Proto-Germanic *azaniz f. Cognate with Middle Dutch arn, Middle Low German erne, arne, Old English *ern (in rugern). The modern form with an alveolar plosive (first attested in Middle High German ernde f) stems from merger with related Old High German arnōt m, from Proto-Germanic *azanōdaz.

noun:Esche.tx: From Middle High German esche f, asch m, from Old High German asca f, asc m, from Proto-West Germanic *ask. The umlaut can be explained here from the plural of the masculine noun, though it may also be due to the secondary umlaut triggered by following -sch- which is found throughout western dialects of High German (compare Äsche, where this is probably the cause of the umlaut).

noun:Esel.tx: From Middle High German esel, from Old High German esil, from late Proto-West Germanic *asil, which is borrowed from Late Latin asellus.

adj:edel.tx: From Middle High German edel, adel, from Old High German adal, from Proto-West Germanic *aþal, Proto-Germanic *aþalaz, see also Old English æþel- (> English athel), Old Norse aðall.

verb:erkennen.tx: From Middle High German erkennen, from Old High German irkennen, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀkannijan. Equivalent to er- + kennen.

noun:Einhorn.tx: From Middle High German einhorn, einhurne, from Old High German einhorn(o), einhurn(o), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *ainahorn, a calque of Latin ūnicornis, itself a calque of Ancient Greek μονόκερως (monókerōs). Equivalent to ein + Horn.

verb:erlauben.tx: From Middle High German erlouben, from Old High German irlouben, arlouben, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀlaubijan, from Proto-Germanic *uzlaubijaną. Cognate with Old English ālīefan, ālȳfan (“to allow”). More at leave (“permission”).

verb:erteilen.tx: From Middle High German erteilen, from Old High German irteilen, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀdailijan. Equivalent to er- + teilen.

verb:erlöschen.tx: er- + löschen, but the intransitive usage from erleschen from Middle High German erleschen.

adj:eben.tx: The adjective is from Middle High German ëben, from Old High German ëban, the adverb from ëbano; from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz and its adverb equivalent. Cognate with Low German even, Dutch even, effen, English even, Danish jævn.

adv:eben.tx: The adjective is from Middle High German ëben, from Old High German ëban, the adverb from ëbano; from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz and its adverb equivalent. Cognate with Low German even, Dutch even, effen, English even, Danish jævn.

intj:eben.tx: The adjective is from Middle High German ëben, from Old High German ëban, the adverb from ëbano; from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz and its adverb equivalent. Cognate with Low German even, Dutch even, effen, English even, Danish jævn.

noun:Ebene.tx: From Middle High German ëbene, from Old High German ëbanī, derived from ëban (“plane, smooth”), from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz. By surface analysis, eben + -e (noun-forming suffix). The mathematical sense is a semantic loan from Latin planum. Others have been influenced by French niveau and English level.

adj:eitel.tx: From Middle High German ītel (“empty, void, vain”), from Old High German ītal (“empty”), from Proto-West Germanic *īdl. Cognate with Luxembourgish eidel (“empty”), Dutch ijdel (“vain”), English idle.

adj:erste.tx: From Middle High German ērest, from Old High German ērist, from Proto-West Germanic *airist.

det:euer.tx: From Middle High German iuwer, from Old High German iuwar. Compare English your, Dutch jouw, uw.

noun:Eingeweide.tx: From Middle High German ingeweide, from earlier geweide, a word restricted to High German. Predominantly attributed to hunter’s jargon as a derivation from Weide (“food, pasture”), as some of the guts are thrown to the dogs. Alternatively related to Weide (“willow”), then in the sense of “something wound up, convoluted”; compare Latin viscera (“entrails”).

verb:erbrechen.tx: From Middle High German erbrëchen, from Old High German irbrëhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀbrekan (“to break apart, shatter”), equivalent to er- + brechen. Cognate with Old English ābrecan, Middle English abreken (“to shatter”).

noun:Erlösung.tx: From Middle High German erlœsunge, from Old High German irlōsunga. Analyzable as erlösen (“to deliver”) + -ung.

noun:Einwohner.tx: Alteration of older Inwohner, from Middle High German inwoner, innewoner. Equivalent to inne- / ein- + wohnen + -er. Compare the verb innewohnen and Dutch inwoner.

verb:entziffern.tx: Calque of French déchiffrer, ent- + ziffern.

verb:erwecken.tx: From Middle High German erwecken, from Old High German irwekken, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀwakkjan. Equivalent to er- + wecken.

noun:Entwicklung.tx: First attested in the 17th century. From entwickeln (“to develop”) + -ung (“-ing”). Likely a calque of French développement.

noun:Enzym.tx: Coined by German physiologist Wilhelm Friedrich Kühne in 1878. From Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + ζύμη (zúmē, “sourdough”).

noun:Eiszeit.tx: Eis + Zeit, attributed to Karl Friedrich Schimper.

verb:erscheinen.tx: From Middle High German erschīnen, from Old High German irskīnan, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀskīnan. Equivalent to er- + scheinen.

verb:entwickeln.tx: From ent- (“un-”) + wickeln (“to wrap”). Calque of French développer.

verb:eilen.tx: From Middle High German īlen, from Old High German īlen, from Proto-West Germanic *īlijan (“to make haste, hasten”).

noun:Elfe.tx: Borrowed in the 18th century from English elf, from Old English ælf (“incubus, elf”), from Proto-West Germanic *albi, from Proto-Germanic *albiz. Compare German Alb (“two-faced spirit”).

noun:Erpel.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German erpel, which is borrowed from Middle Dutch erpel (introduced by Flemish settlers in the East), probably a pet form of the Old Saxon personal name Erpo or Old High German Erpho (literally “the brown one”), from Proto-Germanic *erpaz (“brown”). The word is not part of modern standard Dutch.

noun:Elektrizität.tx: Ultimately from the same Ancient Greek word for "amber" as electron.

noun:Eistee.tx: From Eis (“ice”) + Tee (“tea”). Calque of English ice tea.

adj:einmalig.tx: From einmal + -ig. Cognate with Dutch eenmalig.

verb:ergötzen.tx: From Middle High German ergetzen (“to cause to forget”), from Old High German irgezzen, hence “to compensate, to reimburse”. The verb is a causative to a lost Middle High German ergëȥȥen which existed alongside vergëȥȥen, whence modern vergessen (“to forget”); the simplex verb *getzen is also lost. The spelling with ⟨ö⟩ first arises in the 16th century, but the older form ergetzen also persists …

noun:Empfänger.tx: From Middle High German enpfengære, enphengære, entvengære, equivalent to empfangen + -er.

verb:ergeben.tx: From Middle High German ergëben, from Old High German irgëban, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀgeban, Proto-Germanic *uzgebaną; cognate with obsolete English agive. Equivalent to er- + geben.

verb:empfangen.tx: From Middle High German enphāhen, from Old High German intvāhan, from Proto-Germanic *andfanhaną. Equivalent to emp- + fangen and further ent- + fangen. Cognate with Dutch ontvangen, Old Saxon antfāhan.

verb:exorzieren.tx: From Medieval Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō, “to banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos).

adj:endlich.tx: From Middle High German endelīch (“final”), equivalent to Ende (“end”) + -lich (“-ly”). See English endly.

adv:endlich.tx: From Middle High German endelīch (“final”), equivalent to Ende (“end”) + -lich (“-ly”). See English endly.

noun:Eisberg.tx: From Eis (“ice”) + Berg (“mountain”), a calque of Dutch ijsberg.

noun:Eskalation.tx: Borrowed from English escalation, equivalent to eskalieren + -ation.

verb:einschüchtern.tx: ein- + schüchtern + -en, calque of Latin intimidō.

noun:Eszett.tx: From Es (“S”) + Zett (“Z”), since the letter was initially a ligature of ſ (the long s) and z (with a shape similar to ʒ).

verb:erwachen.tx: From Middle High German erwachen, from Old High German irwahhēn, urwahhēn. Equivalent to er- + wachen.

noun:Erdnussbutter.tx: Erdnuss + Butter, calque of English peanut butter.

adj:empfindlich.tx: From Middle High German enphintlich, from Old High German inphintlich, equivalent to empfinden + -lich.

noun:Eigentum.tx: From Middle High German eigentuom. Equivalent to eigen (“own”) + -tum (“-dom”), compare Dutch eigendom.

adj:extraterrestrisch.tx: From extra- + terrestrisch, modeled on or cognate with English extraterrestrial.

verb:erinnern.tx: From Middle High German erinnern, erinneren, from er- + innern from Old High German innarōn (“to make someone perceive inwardly”), from innar (“inner”), see the preposition in (“in”).

verb:erröten.tx: From Middle High German errōten, from Old High German irrotēn. Equivalent to er- + röten.

verb:ermüden.tx: From Middle High German ermüeden, from Old High German irmuodēn. Equivalent to er- + müde + -en.

noun:Enthusiasmus.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin enthusiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós).

verb:erobern.tx: From Middle High German geoberen, oberen, from Old High German giobarōn (“to delay, overcome”), obarōn (“to delay, cancel”), also irobarōn (“to get tired, exhausted”). Related to obere (“upper”).

verb:einnehmen.tx: From Middle High German īnnëmen, from Old High German innëman. By surface analysis, ein + nehmen.

adv:ebenfalls.tx: Univerbation from earlier adverbial genitive ebenen Falls (literally “just the same case”).

noun:Einheit.tx: From eins (“one”) + -heit; calque of Latin ūnitās. Compare English onehood and Dutch eenheid.

verb:erschrecken.tx: From Middle High German erschrëcken (strong declension), from Old High German irskrëkkan. Equivalent to er- + schrecken.

noun:Effekt.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin effectus. Attested since the 15th century, in common use since the 17th.

noun:Einbruch.tx: Deverbal from einbrechen, equivalent to ein- + Bruch.

noun:Einfluss.tx: From Middle High German īnvluȥ, īnfluȥ, invluȥ, influȥ, from Old High German influȥ, a calque of Old French influence, Latin īnfluēns. By surface analysis, deverbal from einfließen. Also analysable as ein- + Fluss. Compare Middle Low German invlôt, Dutch invloed, English inflood; English inflow.

noun:Energie.tx: From Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia, “action, act, work”), from ἐνεργός (energós, “active”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

verb:erfüllen.tx: From Middle High German ervüllen, from Old High German irfullen, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀfullijan. Equivalent to er- + füllen.

adj:empirisch.tx: Borrowed from Latin empīricus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπειρικός (empeirikós).

noun:Empathie.tx: Borrowed from English empathy, from Ancient Greek ἐμπάθεια (empátheia, literally “passion”).

noun:Etikett.tx: Borrowed from French étiquette. Doublet of Etikette.

noun:Erfahrung.tx: From Middle High German ervarunge, from Old High German irfarunga. By surface analysis, erfahren + -ung.

verb:erfahren.tx: From Middle High German ervarn, from Old High German irfaran, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀfaran. Cognate with Old English āfaran (whence obsolete English afare). By surface analysis, er- + fahren.

adj:erfahren.tx: From Middle High German ervarn, from Old High German irfaran, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀfaran. Cognate with Old English āfaran (whence obsolete English afare). By surface analysis, er- + fahren.

verb:ersetzen.tx: From Middle High German ersetzen, from Old High German irsezzen. By surface analysis, er- + setzen.

verb:enttäuschen.tx: Late 18th century, from ent- (“un-, dis-”) + täuschen (“to deceive”), a calque of French détromper (“to disillusion”), which had earlier been borrowed as detrompi(e)ren (now obsolete).

verb:entschuldigen.tx: From Middle High German entschuldigen (“to absolve, exonerate”). By surface analysis, ent- (“de-, dis-”) + schuldig (“guilty”) + -en, literally “to exculpate”.

verb:erwarten.tx: From er- + warten. Compare Dutch verwachten.

verb:einführen.tx: ein- + führen. Cognate with Scottish English infare.

noun:Egoismus.tx: Borrowed from New Latin egoismus, from Latin ego.

noun:Einspruch.tx: 15th century, verbal noun of archaic einsprechen (“to object”). Equivalent to ein- (“in”) + Spruch (“dictum, statement”).

intj:Einspruch.tx: 15th century, verbal noun of archaic einsprechen (“to object”). Equivalent to ein- (“in”) + Spruch (“dictum, statement”).

verb:eskalieren.tx: From the root of Eskalation + -ieren, modeled off English escalate. First attested in the late 1960s in the context of the Cold War.

verb:einschlafen.tx: From Middle High German īnslāfen. Equivalent to ein- + schlafen.

verb:entschlafen.tx: From Middle High German entslāfen, from Old High German intslāfan. Equivalent to ent- + schlafen.

verb:erweitern.tx: er- + weitern (“to extend, to expand”, obsolete, derived from the comparative of weit).

adj:enorm.tx: Borrowed from French énorme, from Latin ēnōrmis.

noun:Emaille.tx: Borrowed from French émail, from Old French esmal, from Frankish *smalt, from Proto-West Germanic *smalt. Doublet of Schmalz.

verb:engagieren.tx: Borrowed from French engager, replacing the verb ending with -ieren. Compare English engage, Portuguese engajar.

noun:Ekstase.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin ecstasis, further influenced by French extase.

noun:Einkerbung.tx: From a nominalization of the verb einkerben (“to notch (in / into)”) (ein- + kerben) (thus Einkerbung = ein- + kerb- + -ung).

verb:ernennen.tx: From Middle High German ernennen. Equivalent to er- + nennen.

verb:entspringen.tx: From Middle High German entspringen, from Old High German intspringan. Decomposable as ent- + springen.

verb:einmachen.tx: ein- (“in”) + machen (“make, do, process”); cognate to Dutch inmaken.

verb:erhöhen.tx: From Middle High German erhœhen, erhœgen, from Old High German irhōhen, irhohen, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀhauhijan. Equivalent to er- + hoch + -en. Cognate with Old Dutch irhōen, Middle Low German erhȫgen.

verb:erzwingen.tx: From Middle High German ertwingen, from Old High German irdwingan. Equivalent to er- + zwingen.

verb:exen.tx: Derived from the synonymous phrase (auf) ex trinken, which see.

verb:einstellen.tx: From Middle High German īnstellen. Equivalent to ein- + stellen. Cognate to Dutch instellen.

noun:Enzyklopädie.tx: Variant of earlier Encyclopädie, from New Latin encyclopaedia with influence from French encyclopédie, from Koine Greek ἐγκύκλιος παιδείᾱ (enkúklios paideíā, “education in the circle of arts and sciences”), from Ancient Greek ἐγκύκλιος (enkúklios, “circular”) + παιδείᾱ (paideíā, “childrearing; education”), q.v.

noun:Ehrenwort.tx: From Ehre (“honor”) + Wort (“word”). Cognate of Dutch erewoord.

noun:Entwickler.tx: From ent- (“un-”) + wickeln (“to wrap”) + -er (“-er”) or simply entwickeln + -er (“-er”).

verb:empören.tx: From Middle High German enbœren, from Old High German bor (“height, summit, peak”). See the related empor (“upward”) for more.

verb:erschießen.tx: From Middle High German erschiezen, from Old High German irskiozan. Equivalent to er- + schießen.

adv:empor.tx: With the assimilation -ntb- → -mp- (as in Wimper) from earlier entbor, itself an alteration of Middle High German embor, enbor, enbore, from a phrase en bor (“to(wards) (a) height”), of which the second word is from Old High German bor (“height, summit, peak”). Related to English bear (verb), itself from Proto-Germanic *beraną (“to bear”); see there for more.

noun:E-Mail.tx: Borrowed from English e-mail. The feminine gender probably after Post (“mail”), perhaps also Nachricht (“message”).

noun:Eigenschaft.tx: From Middle High German eigenschaft, from Old High German eiganscaft, eiganskaft, equivalent to eigen (“own”, adjective) + -schaft (“-ship”).

adj:erstklassig.tx: erste + Klasse + -ig. Compare Dutch eersteklas, Swedish förstklassig, Danish førsteklasses.

noun:Einsiedler.tx: From Old High German einsidilo (8th century)

noun:Eremit.tx: Borrowed from Latin eremita, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs, “person of the desert”) from ἐρημία (erēmía, “desert, solitude”), from ἔρημος (érēmos) or ἐρῆμος (erêmos, “uninhabited”) plus -ίτης (-ítēs, “one connected to, a member of”).

noun:Etat.tx: Borrowed from French état. Doublet of Staat and Status.

adj:erbärmlich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German erbarmeclich, from Old High German irbarmalīh. By surface analysis, erbarmen + -lich.

verb:erbarmen.tx: Most likely related to archaic German Barm (“bosom”) and has the sense of "cherishing in one's bosom," from Middle High German barm, from Old High German barm, from Proto-West Germanic *barm. Alternatively, from Middle High German erbarmen, irbarmen, from Old High German irbarmēn (“to take pity, have mercy on”), from Proto-West Germanic *armēn (“to take pity”).

verb:erleiden.tx: From Middle High German erlīden, from Old High German irlīdan. Equivalent to er- + leiden

noun:Ejakulat.tx: Borrowed from New Latin ēiaculātum. By surface analysis, ejakulieren + -at.

noun:Entropie.tx: Coined by Rudolf Clausius in 1865, from Ancient Greek ἐντροπία (entropía, “a turning towards”), after Energie.

verb:etablieren.tx: 17th century, borrowed from French établir, from Latin stabilire (“to confirm, establish”).

verb:erwischen.tx: From Middle High German erwischen. Equivalent to er- + wischen.

noun:Ewigkeit.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ēwicheit, from Old High German ēwigheit. By surface analysis, ewig + -keit. Compare Dutch eeuwigheid.

noun:Etappe.tx: Ca. 1700, from French étape. Doublet of Staffel and Stapel.

noun:Egoist.tx: From French égoïste, from Latin ego + -iste. By surface analysis, Ego + -ist.

noun:Ertrag.tx: From the obsolete verb ertragen (“to yield, bring in”), presumably composed of er- and tragen (“to bear, carry”).

verb:erwidern.tx: From Middle High German erwidern, from Old High German irwidarōn. Equivalent to er- + wider (“against”) + -n.

adv:etwa.tx: From Middle High German etwā, contraction of etewā (also eteswā), from Old High German edde(s)hwār (“somewhere”). For the first component compare etlich, etwas; the second is wo (“where”). A related formation was Middle High German ete(s)wanne, in which the second component is wann (“when”). It yielded modern etwan, which was displaced by the 19th century.

noun:Enterich.tx: From Middle High German antrëche, from Old High German anutrëhho (“male duck, drake”), from Proto-West Germanic *anadrekō (“duck leader”). Cognate with dialectal German Drache (“male duck, drake”), Low German drake (“male duck, drake”), Middle English drake (“male duck”). By surface analysis, Ente + -rich. More at drake.

verb:erwägen.tx: From Middle High German erwëgen, from Old High German irwëgan. Equivalent to er- + wägen.

noun:Epos.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔπος (épos, “word, speech”).

verb:erwerben.tx: From Middle High German erwërben, from Old High German irwërban. Equivalent to er- + werben. Compare Dutch verwerven.

adj:einfältig.tx: From Middle High German einveltec, einvaltic, from Old High German *einfaltīg (suggested by derivatives Old High German einfalto, einfaltīglīhho (adverb)), equivalent to Einfalt + -ig. Compare Old High German einfalt (“simple; sincere”, adjective), Old Frisian enfaldich (> Saterland Frisian eenfooldich), German Low German eenfoldig, Danish enfoldig, Dutch eenvoudig.

adj:elfte.tx: From Middle High German einlift, einleft, eilft, from Old High German einlifto, from Proto-Germanic *ainaliftô. Equivalent to elf + -te.

verb:entfernen.tx: From Middle High German entverren. Analysable as ent- + fern + -en.

verb:entscheiden.tx: From Middle High German entscheiden, equivalent to ent- + scheiden. Cognate with German Low German entscheden, Dutch ontscheiden, Saterland Frisian undskede.

adj:einsam.tx: From ein + -sam, probably on the model of gemeinsam.

verb:entkommen.tx: From Middle High German entkomen; ent- + kommen.

verb:erhitzen.tx: From Middle High German erhitzen, from Old High German irhizzen. Equivalent to er- + hitzen.

adj:einzig.tx: From Middle High German einzec, einzic (“single”), ultimately from ein (“one”); see there for more (DWDS).

adv:einzig.tx: From Middle High German einzec, einzic (“single”), ultimately from ein (“one”); see there for more (DWDS).

noun:Eisvogel.tx: From Middle High German īsvogel, from Old High German īsfogal; compare Dutch ijsvogel, Icelandic ísfugl. By surface analysis, Eis + Vogel. The former stem, however, is considered to be a variant of Eisen (Old High German īsarn), most likely referring to the green-blue upperparts with pale azure-blue back and rump of the adult bird. But compare parallel Czech ledňáček, Russian леди́нник (ledínnik) …

verb:einbalsamieren.tx: ein- + balsamieren, since the end of the 16th century.

noun:Einsatz.tx: From Middle High German īnsaz. By surface analysis, ein- + Satz. Compare Dutch inzet, English inset.

verb:einsetzen.tx: From Middle High German īnsetzen, insetzen, from Old High German insezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *insattjan. Equivalent to ein- + setzen. Compare English inset.

noun:Entwurf.tx: Nominalization of entwerfen (“to design”). Compare Dutch ontwerp.

verb:entwaffnen.tx: From Middle High German entwāfenen, entwāpenen; equivalent to ent- + waffnen.

verb:entschärfen.tx: ent- (“de-”) + schärfen (“sharpen”). Compare take the edge off, blunt.

verb:erfreuen.tx: From Middle High German ervröuwen, ervröwen, from Old High German irfrewen. Equivalent to er- + freuen.

noun:Exempel.tx: From Middle High German exempel, from Latin exemplum.

verb:entzweien.tx: From earlier Middle High German zweien, Old High German zweiōn (“split in two, divide”), with additional prefix. By surface analysis, ent- + zwei + -en.

adj:exzentrisch.tx: From Medieval Latin excentricus, compare eccentros, ἔκκεντρος (ékkentros).

verb:eröffnen.tx: From Middle High German eroffenen, from Old High German iroffanōn. Equivalent to er- + öffnen.

adj:ernsthaft.tx: From Middle High German ernesthaft, from Old High German ernusthafti. By surface analysis, Ernst (“seriousness”) + -haft (“adjectival suffix”).

adv:ernsthaft.tx: From Middle High German ernesthaft, from Old High German ernusthafti. By surface analysis, Ernst (“seriousness”) + -haft (“adjectival suffix”).

verb:empfehlen.tx: From Middle High German enpfelhen, enphelhen, entfelhen, intfelhen, from Old High German intfelhan, intfelahan, from int- + felhan (“to preserve; entrust; confide in; surrender”), with assimilation before f- (see emp-). Equivalent to emp- + fehlen and ent- + fehlen. Related to German befehlen (“command, order”), but not fehlen (“to be missing”).

noun:Ebenbild.tx: From Middle High German ebenbilde, from Old High German ebanbilidi. By surface analysis, eben + Bild.

noun:Erzählung.tx: From er- (“or-: out, resulting from”) + zählen (“tell”) + -ung (“-ing: forming nouns from verbs”).

verb:erreichen.tx: From Middle High German erreichen, from Old High German irreihhen, irreihhōn. Equivalent to er- + reichen.

verb:evakuieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin ēvacuāre (“to empty out”), from ē- + vacuus; compare English evacuate.

verb:ergießen.tx: From Middle High German ergieȥen, from Old High German irgioȥan. Equivalent to er- + gießen.

noun:Empfang.tx: From Middle High German antvanc, from Old High German antfang. By surface analysis, deverbal from empfangen.

noun:Elixier.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin elixir, from Arabic اَلْإِكْسِير (al-ʔiksīr), from Ancient Greek ξηρίον (xēríon, “medicinal powder”), from ξηρός (xērós, “dry”).

adj:eventuell.tx: Borrowed from New Latin eventualis, partly through French éventuel.

adv:eventuell.tx: Borrowed from New Latin eventualis, partly through French éventuel.

adj:extrovertiert.tx: By analogy with introvertiert and extravertiert.

verb:einschalten.tx: From ein- + schalten, perhaps modelled after ausschalten.

adj:erblich.tx: From Middle High German erbelich. Equivalent to Erbe or erben + -lich.

adj:ethnisch.tx: Chiefly since 19th century, from Ancient Greek ἔθνος (éthnos) + -isch, after ἐθνικός (ethnikós) and their descendants Latin ethnicus, French ethnique. The pronunciation with /eː/ was probably influenced by the fact that, until 1901, th often indicated the length of adjacent vowels (like Muth, That etc.).

noun:Ergonomie.tx: ergo- + -nomie, from Polish ergonomia, coined in 1857 by Wojciech Jastrzębowski by combining Ancient Greek ἔργον (érgon) + νόμος (nómos).

noun:Elfmeter.tx: From elf (“eleven”) + Meter (“meter”) (the distance from the penalty spot to the goal).

verb:erfinden.tx: From Middle High German ervinden, from Old High German irfindan, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀfinþan. Equivalent to er- + finden.

noun:Eitelkeit.tx: From Middle High German ītelkeit, ītelcheit, shortened variants of Middle High German ītelicheit, ītellīcheit, ītellichheit, equivalent to eitel + -keit. Cognate with Middle Low German îdelichhêt, Dutch ijdelheid, English idlehood.

verb:entstehen.tx: From Middle High German entstēn, entstān, from Old High German intstantan, intstantēn, intstantēn. Equivalent to ent- (“start”) + stehen (“stand”).

verb:ertrinken.tx: From Middle High German ertrinken, from Old High German irtrinkan, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀdrinkan. By surface analysis, er- + trinken.

verb:empfinden.tx: Inherited from Middle High German enpfinden, entfinden, from Old High German intfindan. Equivalent to emp- + finden and ent- + finden.

verb:einladen.tx: From Middle High German īnladen, from Old High German inladōn, inladēn, from in- + ladōn, ladēn (“to invite”), from Proto-Germanic *laþōną (“to invite”). The originally weak verb -laden in einladen and vorladen is unrelated to laden (“to load”), but was early on conflated with the latter.

verb:entladen.tx: From Middle High German entladen, from Old High German intladan, intladen, inthladan, inthladen. By surface analysis, ent- + laden.

verb:ereignen.tx: With dialectal unrounding from eräugnen, itself with intrusive -n- from eräugen, from Middle High German eröugen, from Old High German irougen (“to show”). Es ereignet sich is thus “it shows itself”. Equivalent to er- + Auge + -en.

verb:erschüttern.tx: Intensive form of obsolete erschütten, from Middle High German erschütten, erschüten, from Old High German irscutten. Synchronically analyzable as er- + schüttern, the latter component an iterative of schütten (“to pour, stream down”).

noun:Eselsbrücke.tx: From Esel (“donkey”) + -s- + Brücke (“bridge”), a calque of Latin pōns asinōrum. Apparently attested in German from the 18th c. Compare the same in Dutch ezelsbrug.

verb:erwähnen.tx: 16th century, alteration of earlier gewähnen, from Middle High German gewähenen, gewahen, from Old High German giwahanen, giwahan, from Proto-West Germanic *gawahwan (“to say, mention”).

noun:Evangelium.tx: Borrowed from Latin euangelium, evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion).

verb:ernten.tx: From Middle High German ernen, arnen, from Old High German arnōn, from Proto-Germanic *azanōną. This verb is denominal from the noun *azaniz (“harvest”), which underwent umlaut in inflected forms and was later merged with a related noun to yield modern German Ernte. The verb was continuously adapted to its underlying noun.

verb:evaluieren.tx: From French évaluer. Compare Dutch evalueren, Swedish evaluera, Danish evaluere.

adv:eigentlich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German eigenlīche, equivalent to eigen + -lich. Compare Dutch eigenlijk.

adj:eigentlich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German eigenlīche, equivalent to eigen + -lich. Compare Dutch eigenlijk.

verb:erörtern.tx: From er- + Middle High German örtern (“to examine carefully”), itself a verbal form from örter, the plural of ort (“outermost point in space and time, tip, end; place”), thus "to follow through to the tip (of a thing)" > "to examine thoroughly" > "to discuss". See Ort (“place”) for more.

noun:Eiland.tx: From Middle High German eilant, einlant, from Middle Low German eilant (by which it was reinforced again during the 16th c.), from Old Frisian eiland, from Proto-West Germanic *auwjuland, from Proto-Germanic *awjōlandą. Cognate with Dutch eiland, English island, Icelandic eyland.

verb:einleiten.tx: From Middle High German īnleiten, from Old High German inleiten, from Proto-West Germanic *inlaidijan, from Proto-Germanic *inlaidijaną. Equivalent to ein- + leiten. Cognates include Dutch inleiden and English inlead.

noun:Ethik.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin ēthica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).

verb:entfremden.tx: From Middle High German enphremden, entvremden. ent- + fremd.

verb:erstechen.tx: From Middle High German erstechen, from Old High German irstehhan. Equivalent to er- + stechen.

noun:Einbildung.tx: From Middle High German īnbildunge (“imprinting”). By surface analysis, einbilden + -ung.

noun:Edikt.tx: Borrowed from Latin ēdictum (“proclamation, edict”), the neuter of ēdictus, perfect passive participle of ēdīcō (“to publish, proclaim”), itself from ex (“out of, from”) + dīcō (“say”).

noun:Erythem.tx: Borrowed from New Latin erythēma, from Ancient Greek ἐρύθημα (erúthēma, “a redness or flush on the skin”), from ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”).

verb:eingehen.tx: From Middle High German īngān, from Old High German ingān, from Proto-West Germanic *ingān. Analyzable as ein- + gehen.

verb:enthalten.tx: From Middle High German enthalten, equivalent to ent- + halten. Influenced by innehalten, einhalten (literally “to hold inside”). This is clearest in the sense “to contain”, compare Inhalt (“contents”); but it is possible even in the sense “to abstain”, compare mit etwas einhalten (“to stop”), sich einhalten (“to restrain oneself”). Cognate with Dutch onthouden (“to remember, withhold”) and …

adj:enthalten.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

conj:entweder.tx: From Middle High German eintwëder, einwëder, Old High German einwedar, einhwedar. The first part is unrelated to ent-, but rather a reduced form of the pronoun ein to which the -t was seemingly only added in Middle High German, with weder as the second part.

verb:enden.tx: From Middle High German enden, from Old High German entōn, from Proto-West Germanic *andijōn. Equivalent to Ende + -en.

adj:endlos.tx: From Middle High German endelos, from Old High German endilōs, from Proto-Germanic *andijalausaz. Structurally Ende (“end”) + -los (“-less”)

noun:Eindruck.tx: From Middle High German īndruc, a calque of Latin impressio. Equivalent to ein- + Druck. Compare Dutch indruk.

adj:erdig.tx: From Middle High German erdic, erdec, also irdic, irdec, equivalent to Erde + -ig.

noun:Erdkunde.tx: 18th century, from Erde + -kunde, a calque of Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).

noun:Entzug.tx: ent- + Zug; nominal form of entziehen (“to deprive, withdraw, revoke”).

noun:Eukalyptus.tx: 19th century, learned borrowing from New Latin eucalyptus, coined by L’Héritier after Ancient Greek εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + καλυπτός (kaluptós, “covered”).

noun:Eibe.tx: From Middle High German īwe, from Old High German īwa, from Proto-West Germanic *īwā, īhwā, *īhu, from Proto-Germanic *īwō, *īhwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyHw-. Cognate with dated Dutch ijf, English yew, Lithuanian ievà, Russian ива (iva). Middle High German postvocalic -w- was normally lost. It has been preserved in ewig, Löwe, and with secondary hardening to -b- in Eibe and Hieb.

noun:Elegie.tx: Borrowed from Middle French elegie, from Latin elegīa, from Ancient Greek ἐλεγείᾱ (elegeíā), ellipsis of ἐλεγείᾱ ᾠδή (elegeíā ōidḗ, “an elegiac song”).

adv:eher.tx: Chiefly from haplology of Middle High German ērer, from Old High German ēriro, from Proto-Germanic *airizô. Compare Dutch eerder. Likely conflated with Middle High German ēr, a rarer byform of ē (whence modern eh, ehe), from Old High German ēr, from Proto-Germanic *airiz, adverbial form of the above. Cognate with Dutch eer, English ere, Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌹𐍃 (airis). The final /r/ was regularly lost in …

noun:Eibisch.tx: From Middle High German ībesche, from Old High German ībisca, from Proto-West Germanic *ībisku, from Late Latin ibīscum, hībiscum. Doublet of Hibiskus.

noun:Eileiter.tx: From Ei (“egg”) + Leiter (“ladder/conductor”), from leiten (“to lead”).

verb:erstehen.tx: From Middle High German erstān, erstēn, from Old High German irstantan, irstān, irstēn, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀstān. Equivalent to er- + stehen.

verb:erlassen.tx: From Middle High German erlāzen, from Old High German irlāzan, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀlātan. Equivalent to er- + lassen.

verb:erledigen.tx: From Middle High German erledigen. Equivalent to er- + ledig + -en.

verb:entsetzen.tx: From Middle High German entsezzen, from Old High German intsezzen. Equivalent to ent- + setzen, literally “to put out (of a state, condition)”, whence the two senses of to horrify (i.e. put out of tranquility) and to relieve (i.e. put out of a siege). Compare Dutch ontzetten.

noun:Erzherzog.tx: From erz- + Herzog. Calque of Latin archidux. First attested in c. 1650.

noun:Einzelhandel.tx: einzeln (“single, piecewise”) + Handel (“trade”). In use by the 17th century, initially in the sense of "monopoly". The sense of "selling directly to the consumer" was established by the 19th century.

pron:etliche.tx: From Middle High German etelich, (also eteslich), from Old High German etelīh, ettalīh (“some; any”), from earlier Old High German eddehwelih, eddeshwelih.

noun:Einverständnis.tx: ein- (“into”) + Verständnis (“understanding, comprehension”, from verstehen “to understand” + -nis “-ness”)

verb:eingeben.tx: From Middle High German īngeben, from Old High German ingeban. Equivalent to ein- + geben. Compare Scots ingive.

verb:erlangen.tx: From Middle High German erlangen. Equivalent to er- + langen.

verb:enthüllen.tx: From ent- + hüllen. Compare Dutch onthullen, English unhill, Gothic 𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌷𐌿𐌻𐌾𐌰𐌽 (andhuljan).

verb:erben.tx: From Middle High German erben, from Old High German *erben, from Proto-West Germanic *arbijan, from Proto-Germanic *arbijaną, denominative from *arbiją.

noun:Einkauf.tx: From Middle High German einkauf. By synchronic analysis, the deverbal noun of einkaufen (“to shop”).

adj:elliptisch.tx: From Latin ellīpticus + -isch, from Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós, “defective”).

verb:einholen.tx: From Middle High German īnholn. Equivalent to ein- + holen.

noun:Eberesche.tx: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ebʰros (“yew”). Cognate with Proto-Celtic *eburos, Albanian bërshen.

verb:einchecken.tx: Calque of English check in, equivalent to ein- + checken.

verb:erlösen.tx: From Middle High German erlœsen, from Old High German irlōsen, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀlausijan, from Proto-Germanic *uzlausijaną. By surface analysis, er + lösen (“to loosen”).

adj:exaltiert.tx: Past participle of sich exaltieren (“to become hysterical”), from French s'exalter (“to be elated”).

noun:Eingabe.tx: Deverbal from eingeben. By surface analysis, ein- + Gabe.

noun:Ego-Shooter.tx: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from Latin ego (“I”) + shooter.

noun:Euthanasie.tx: From French euthanasie, from Ancient Greek εὐθανασίᾱ (euthanasíā).

adj:ethisch.tx: From Latin ēthicus, with assimilation to native suffix -isch.

verb:erkälten.tx: From Middle High German erkelten. Analyzable as er- + kalt + -en.

verb:ertränken.tx: From Middle High German ertrenken, from Old High German irtrenken. Equivalent to er- + tränken.

verb:entschädigen.tx: From ent- + schädigen. Compare French dédommager.

verb:entwenden.tx: From Middle High German entwenden. Equivalent to ent- + wenden.

noun:Ehrfurcht.tx: From Ehre + Furcht, since the end of the 16th century.

noun:Eucharistie.tx: From Ecclesiastical Latin eucharistia, from Ancient Greek εὐχαριστία (eukharistía, “gratitude, giving of thanks”).

noun:Estragon.tx: Borrowed from French estragon, metathesized from estargon, from targon, from Medieval Latin tarcon, altarcon, from Arabic طَرْخُون (ṭarḵūn), ultimately from Ancient Greek δρακόντιον (drakóntion), from δράκων (drákōn).

noun:Eigentor.tx: From eigen (“own”) + Tor (“goal”), probably a calque of English own goal.

verb:ebnen.tx: From Middle High German ëbenen, from Old High German ëbanōn. Equivalent to eben (“level”) + -en.

adj:eilig.tx: From Middle High German īlig, from Old High German īlīg, from Proto-West Germanic *īlīg. Equivalent to Eile + -ig.

verb:einloggen.tx: Partial calque of English log in.

noun:Exosphäre.tx: From Ancient Greek ἔξω (éxō, “out (of), outside”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, sphere”).

verb:erziehen.tx: From Middle High German erziehen, from Old High German irziohan, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀteuhan. Equivalent to er- + ziehen.

adj:entflammbar.tx: Derived from the verb entflammen: entflamm- (“to inflame”) + -bar (“-able”). Compare Dutch ontvlambaar.

verb:einwecken.tx: From ein- + Weck + -en, named after German businessman Johann Weck (1841–1914) who began selling the Weck jar at the beginning of the 20th century. The verb is modeled after einkochen or einmachen, common terms for canning food. The company simply replaced -koch- with -weck-, thus making their products more popular.

noun:Epitaph.tx: Borrowed from Latin epitaphium. Compare Middle High German epitafum, epitâfium.

verb:ekeln.tx: 15th century, from Middle Low German ēgelen, ēchelen, ēkelen, from Old Saxon *eglan, from Proto-West Germanic *aglijan (related to English ail). The -k- then likely through influence of Middle Low German ēken, āken (“to suppurate”), from Old Saxon *akan (related to English ache); compare Dutch akelig. An alternative theory sees in the now archaic adjective ekel a northern variant of heikel …

adv:einst.tx: From Middle High German einst, einest, from Old High German einēst, eines (“once”), from ein (“one”). More at once.

verb:eignen.tx: From Middle High German eigenen, Old High German eiganen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aiginōną. Compare English own, Swedish ägna. Related to eigen.

adv:ehemals.tx: From Middle High German ēmāles, ē māles (“formerly”), from ē (“before”) + genitive of māl (“time, occurrence”). Morphologically ehe + Mal + -s.

noun:Echse.tx: Back-formation from Eidechse, possibly misidentifying the first part as Eid (“oath”). Coined in 1816 by Lorenz Oken to describe lizards more generally, as the original term was primarily associated with Lacertae.

noun:Endlösung.tx: From Ende (“end”) + Lösung (“solution”). Even before Hitler (some time in 1941) gave the command for outright genocide, the Nazis had been using the term to refer to an eventual displacement of the Jews from western and central Europe—by emigration and deportation as it was then understood. When the extermination program began, the term was transferred and soon enough restricted to this sense.

verb:einfallen.tx: From Middle High German īnvallen, from Old High German infallan, from Proto-West Germanic *infallan. Equivalent to ein- + fallen.

verb:erholen.tx: From Middle High German erholn, from Old High German irhalо̄n, irholо̄n. Equivalent to er- + holen.

verb:einfangen.tx: From Middle High German īnvāhen, from Old High German infāhan. Equivalent to ein- + fangen.

adj:ellenlang.tx: From Middle High German; equivalent to Ellen (“ells”) + lang (“long”).

verb:entwerfen.tx: From ent- + werfen. Compare Dutch ontwerpen.

verb:ermahnen.tx: From Middle High German ermanen, from Old High German irmanōn. Equivalent to er- + mahnen.

noun:Examen.tx: Borrowed from Latin exāmen in the 16th century.

adj:einzeln.tx: From Middle High German einzel, derived from einez, from Old High German einaz.

adv:einzeln.tx: From Middle High German einzel, derived from einez, from Old High German einaz.

verb:ergreifen.tx: From Middle High German ergreifen, from Old High German irgreifōn. Equivalent to er- + greifen.

verb:ersticken.tx: From Middle High German ersticken, from Old High German irsticken. Equivalent to er- + sticken.

verb:entwischen.tx: From Middle High German entwischen, from Old High German intwisken. Traditionally considered to be a compound of ent- (“away from”) + wischen (“to wipe, scrub”). However, the second component is considered by Cheung to be derived from a different root, Proto-Indo-European *wyedʰ- (“to shoot, take aim, hit, wound”), with Sanskrit व्यध् (vyadh, “to pierce, hit”) and Old Armenian վէրք (vērkʻ, …

verb:erhellen.tx: From Middle High German erhellen. Equivalent to er- + hellen.

verb:erwärmen.tx: From Middle High German erwermen, from Old High German irwermen, irwarmen. Equivalent to er- + wärmen.

noun:Echtzeit.tx: echt (“real”) + Zeit (“time”) Calque of English real-time.

adj:einverstanden.tx: ein- (“into”) + verstanden (past participle of verstehen “to understand”)

adv:ebenso.tx: eben + so. Compare English even so.

intj:ebenso.tx: eben + so. Compare English even so.

verb:einbläuen.tx: From earlier einbleuen (literally “to beat in”), from obsolete bleuen (“to beat”). The spelling with ä comes from a folk etymological association with blau (“blue; bruised”). Equivalent to ein- + bläuen.

verb:einigen.tx: From Middle High German einegen, einigen, from Old High German gieinīgen.

verb:entnehmen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German entnëmen, from Old High German intnëman. Equivalent to ent- (“from”) + nehmen (“take”).

verb:entweichen.tx: From Middle High German entweichen, entwīchen, from Old High German intwīchan. Equivalent to ent- + weichen.

adj:exzellent.tx: Borrowed from Latin excellēns. Cognate with English excellent.

adj:ehern.tx: From Middle High German ēren, ērīn, from Old High German ērīn, derived from ēr (“ore”), from Proto-Germanic *aiz. Not related with Erz (“ore”), but associated with it.

pron:einig.tx: From Middle High German einec, from Old High German einag, einīg, from Proto-West Germanic *ainag. More at any.

adj:einig.tx: From Middle High German einec, from Old High German einag, einīg, from Proto-West Germanic *ainag. More at any.

noun:Endung.tx: From Middle High German endunge, from Old High German entunga, gientunga. Compare Middle Low German endinge, Middle Dutch endinge and eindinge, Old English endung, English ending. By surface analysis, enden + -ung.

adj:eisern.tx: From Middle High German īseren, īserīn, from Old High German īsarnīn, from Proto-Germanic *īsarnīnaz. Equivalent to Eiser (“iron”), older variant of Eisen + -en. Now reanalysable as Eisen (“iron”) + -ern, but historically eisern is itself one of the words that contributed to the development of this extended suffix -ern (see there).

verb:erachten.tx: From Middle High German erahten, from Old High German irahtōn. Equivalent to er- + achten.

verb:ehren.tx: From Middle High German ēren, from Old High German ēren, from Proto-Germanic *aizāną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eys- (“to respect”).

adj:etepetete.tx: Borrowed from German Low German. A reduplication of öte (“affected, finical”), dialectally ete, possibly influenced by French peut-être (“maybe”).

adj:elend.tx: From Middle High German ellende, contracted from Old High German elilenti, from Proto-West Germanic *alljas (“other”) + *land (“land”). The modern form with a long vowel is based on Middle Low German elende and/or other regional variants. Today pronounced also with a secondary full vowel in the second syllable. Cognate to Dutch ellende (noun).

verb:erübrigen.tx: From er- + übrig (“remaining, left over”) + -en, hence “to leave over, have as surplus”. Accordingly, the reflexive sich erübrigen actually means “to be left, remain” and one would originally say es erübrigt sich, etwas zu tun in the sense of “XY still remains to be done”. The quite opposite contemporary sense seems to emerge around 1900. It probably developed through confusion with the active …

verb:erdrücken.tx: From Middle High German erdrücken, from Old High German irdrukken. Equivalent to er- + drücken (“to press, squeeze”).

adj:einheimisch.tx: From Middle High German inheimisch, itself analyzable as in- + Heim + -isch. Compare Dutch inheems.

verb:erschlagen.tx: From Middle High German erslahen, from Old High German irslahan, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀslahan. Equivalent to er- + schlagen.

verb:einhalten.tx: From ein- + halten, an alteration of innehalten, which used to have the same senses, but has since been restricted to “pause, wait”. Compare also enthalten.

verb:erhärten.tx: From Middle High German erherten, from Old High German irherten. Equivalent to er- + härten.

verb:entflohen.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

noun:Emphase.tx: From French emphase, from Latin emphasis, from Ancient Greek ἔμφασις (émphasis).

noun:Erythrozyt.tx: From Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”) and κύτος (kútos, “vessel, jar”).

verb:erarbeiten.tx: From Middle High German erarbeiten. Equivalent to er- + arbeiten.

verb:erlegen.tx: From Middle High German erleggen, from Old High German arleggen, irleccen, from Proto-Germanic *uzlagjaną. Equivalent to er- + legen. Cognate with English allay.

adv:euretwegen.tx: Shortened from von euretwegen, which can be traced through two developmental routes. One route is from von eurentwegen / von eurent wegen, from von euren wegen, from Middle High German von iuwern wegen, in which wegen was the dative plural of modern-day Weg and iuwern was the possessive pronoun in the dative plural. Another route can be traced from von euertwegen / von euert wegen, from von euer …

noun:Eintracht.tx: From Middle High German eintraht, which is a borrowing and phonetic adaptation of Middle Low German ēndracht. By surface analysis, ein (“one”) + Tracht (“load, burden”).

noun:Effekten.tx: 17th century, borrowed from Italian effetti, then adapted (via forms like Effecti) to the German cognate Effekt (etymology 2 below). Usage was also influenced by French effets.

verb:erkalten.tx: From Middle High German erkalten, from Old High German irkaltēn, irkaltōn. Equivalent to er- + kalt + -en.

verb:ersuchen.tx: From Middle High German ersuochen, from Old High German irsuohhen, ursuohhen, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀsōkijan, from Proto-Germanic *uzsōkijaną. Equivalent to er- + suchen.

verb:entlehnen.tx: From Middle High German entlēhenen. By surface analysis, ent- (“un-, out-, off-”) + lehnen (“to borrow, lend”).

verb:erlesen.tx: From Middle High German erlësen, from Old High German irlësan, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀlesan. By surface analysis, er- + lesen.

verb:entsinnen.tx: From Middle High German entsinnen; equivalent to ent- + sinnen.

adj:erkenntlich.tx: From Middle High German erkentlich (compare erkennelich and erkantlich). Equivalent to erkennen + -lich.

verb:entrümpeln.tx: Back-formation from Gerümpel with prefix ent-.

noun:Eigenbrötler.tx: From Alemannic German (standard 19th century). Equivalent to eigen + Brot + -ler, literally “own-breader”, originally referring to a bachelor with his own household; compare Middle High German eigen brōt in the sense of “own household”.

verb:eichen.tx: From Middle High German eichen, īchen, from Old High German *īkōn, from Proto-West Germanic *īkwōn (“to measure, gauge”).

adj:eichen.tx: From Middle High German eichīn, from Old High German eihhīn, from Proto-Germanic *aikīnaz, equivalent to Eiche + -en.

noun:Estrich.tx: From Middle High German esterich, estrich, from Old High German estrih, asterih, from Late Latin astracum, astricum, from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “potsherd”).

noun:Esswaren.tx: Compound of either essen (“to eat”) or Essen (“food”) + Waren (“wares, goods”).

verb:entwirren.tx: From Middle High German entwërren. Analyzable as ent- + wirr + -en.

noun:Einfahrt.tx: From Middle High German īnvart, from Old High German infart. By surface analysis, deverbal from einfahren.

verb:erraten.tx: From Middle High German erraten, from Old High German irrātan, arrātan, urrātan, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀrādan, from Proto-Germanic *uzrēdaną (“to guess”). Equivalent to er- + raten (“advise, recommend; guess”). Cognate with English arread.

verb:entjungfern.tx: From Jungfer (in the dated sense of “virgin”) with the prefix ent- (“de-”); thus literally “to devirginize”.

noun:Erdanziehungskraft.tx: Erde (“earth”) + Anziehungskraft (“force of attraction”) or Erdanziehung + -s- + Kraft.

noun:Erlöser.tx: From Middle High German erlœsære, from Old High German irlōsāri, urlōsāri. Analyzable as erlösen (“to deliver”) + -er.

noun:Ecker.tx: The now rare simplex Ecker from Middle High German ackeran, eckern; only once attested in Old High German ekarn. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *akraną, whence also English acorn. An original neuter or masculine whose final -n was interpreted as a plural morpheme and which was subsequently made into a feminine. Kluge (24th edition) considers it a chiefly Low German word (compare Middle Low German …

noun:Einöde.tx: From Middle High German einœte, einœde, from Old High German einōti, from Proto-West Germanic *ainōdī (“wilderness; loneliness”), contaminated with unrelated öde.

noun:Eisbein.tx: From Middle High German īsbein, from Old High German īsbein, from Proto-West Germanic *īsabain.

verb:entern.tx: Via German Low German from Middle Low German entern, itself (probably via Middle Dutch enteren) from Spanish entrar. Compare modern Dutch enteren.

noun:Erlkönig.tx: Calque of Danish ellerkonge (“king of the elves”), in which eller- was misinterpreted as German Low German Eller (“alder”), and which was thus translated into standard German as Erlkönig (Erle + König). This form was spread by Goethe’s famous poem, Erlkönig (1782). German Low German Eller is from Middle Low German elre, from Old Saxon elis.

noun:Espe.tx: From Middle High German aspe, from Old High German aspa, from Proto-West Germanic *aspu. The modern vocalism is from Middle Low German espe, in which it is generalized from derivatives with umlaut. Cognate with Dutch esp.

verb:entblößen.tx: From Middle High German enblœzen. By surface analysis, ent- + bloß + -en.

noun:Edelmann.tx: From Middle High German edelman, from Old High German edilman. Equivalent to edel (“noble, gallant”) + Mann (“man”).

adj:entgeistert.tx: Participle of the archaic verb entgeistern.

verb:erdenken.tx: From Middle High German erdenken, from Old High German irdenken, irthenken, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀþankijan. By surface analysis, er- + denken.

noun:Enzian.tx: From Old High German encian, variant of genciane, from Latin gentiana.

adj:erlaucht.tx: Calque of Latin illūstris. From Middle High German erliuht, from erlūht, past participle of erliuhten (“to illuminate, enlighten”).

verb:evangelisieren.tx: From Latin evangelizō, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελίζω (euangelízō), + -ieren.

verb:ergehen.tx: Middle High German ergēn, ergān, from Old High German irgēn, irgān, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀgān. Equivalent to er- + gehen.

noun:Ern.tx: From Middle High German eren (“floor”), ern, from Old High German erin, arin. Cognate with Icelandic arinn and Danish arne.

adj:eintönig.tx: ein- (“one”) + Ton (“tone, note”) + -ig (“y”). Compare English one-note.

verb:ersinnen.tx: From Middle High German ersinnen, equivalent to er- + sinnen.

noun:Erbfeind.tx: From Middle High German erbevīnt (“the Devil as the hereditary enemy of mankind”). Equivalent to Erbe (“inheritance, heritage”) + Feind (“enemy”). Since the 15th century used of the Turks (seen as infidel and followers of the Devil). Then generalised to any long-standing enmity without religious context. The new narrowing to the French is an influence of 19th-century nationalism, which resented …

adj:emsig.tx: From Middle High German emzec, emzic, from Old High German emezzīg, emizzīg (“persistent, continuous”), attested since the 8th century, of uncertain ultimate origin. Kluge initially suggested that it could be related to Emse (“ant”), but this was later qualified as “uncertain” and removed in subsequent editions.

verb:erfragen.tx: From Middle High German ervrāgen, from Old High German irfrāgēn. Equivalent to er- + fragen.

verb:enterben.tx: From Middle High German enterben, from Old High German interben. Equivalent to ent- + erben.

verb:entbinden.tx: From Middle High German entbinden, enbinden, from Old High German intbintan, from Proto-Germanic *andabindaną. Cognate with English unbind, Dutch ontbinden.

verb:erbauen.tx: From Middle High German erbouwen. Equivalent to er- + bauen.

verb:erzen.tx: From er + -zen, in analogy with duzen and siezen.

verb:einheizen.tx: By surface analysis, ein- + heizen, literally “to heat in”.

noun:Emporkömmling.tx: Calque of French parvenu. By surface analysis, emporkommen + -ling.

adj:ebenbürtig.tx: From Middle High German ëbenbürtec, equivalent to eben + (Ge)burt + -ig ("of even/equal birth").

adj:eingeboren.tx: From Middle High German īnborn, īngeborn. By surface analysis, ein- + geboren.

adj:einhellig.tx: From Middle High German einhellec. Equivalent to ein- (“one”) + hallen (“to sound”) + -ig.

adj:einmütig.tx: From Middle High German einmüetec, from Old High German einmuotig. By surface analysis, eins + Mut + -ig.

adj:emphatisch.tx: From French emphatique, from Latin emphaticus, from Ancient Greek ἐμφατικός (emphatikós). Equivalent to Emphase + -isch.

noun:Emoji.tx: Borrowed from English emoji or its source, Japanese 絵文字(えもじ) (emoji).

adj:entzwei.tx: From Middle High German enzwei, entzwī, inzwī, untzwī, from Old High German in zwei. The first syllable does not originate from the prefix ent-, but was obviously influenced by it (compare the verb entzweien). Cognate with Middle Low German entwei, intwei, untwey.

adj:erhaben.tx: Obsolete perfect passive participle of erheben.

adj:erpicht.tx: Perfect passive participle to an obsolete erpichen (“to coat with pitch”) from Pech (“pitch”).

adj:espen.tx: From Middle High German espīn, derived from aspe (“aspen”). Analyzable as Espe + -en.

noun:Erdferkel.tx: From Erde (“earth”) + Ferkel (“piglet”), after South African Dutch aardvarken. First described in German by Peter Kolbe in 1719, who called it Erdschwein, a more literal calque. The form Erdferkel uses a word that is cognate with Dutch varken (“pig”) but has a slightly different sense.

verb:einsaugen.tx: From Middle High German īnsūgen, from Old High German *insūgan, from Proto-West Germanic *insūgan, equivalent to ein- + saugen. Cognate with German Low German insugen, Dutch inzuigen, English insuck.

noun:Enge.tx: Inherited from Middle High German enge.

noun:Eidam.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German eidam, from Proto-West Germanic *aiþum.

phrase:Ende Gelände.tx: Literally, “end (of) terrain”. The rhyme has a reinforcing effect.

verb:erforschen.tx: From Middle High German ervorschen, from Old High German irforskōn. Equivalent to er- + forschen.
